A1.text:
Kimchi and Plastic.
Kimchi is a Korean food.
People make it from vegetables.
Cabbage is the most common one.
Many people eat kimchi because it is good for the stomach.
Today there is a big problem.
Very small pieces of plastic are everywhere.
We call them microplastics.
They are in our water and our food.
They can go into the body.
Scientists in Korea did a study.
They found a tiny living thing in kimchi.
In the study, this tiny thing holds the plastic.
Then the plastic leaves the body.
But the scientists tested mice, not people.
This is interesting news.
But kimchi is not the answer.
The world still makes too much plastic.
We must make less plastic.
Eating kimchi alone is not enough.

A2.text:
Kimchi and Microplastics.
Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish.
It is made from fermented vegetables, usually cabbage or radish.
Many people eat it because it is healthy and good for the stomach.
These days, scientists are worried about microplastics.
Microplastics are very small pieces of plastic.
They appear when larger plastic breaks down over time.
Now they are in our food, our water, and even our bodies.
Recently, researchers in South Korea made an interesting discovery.
They found a kind of bacteria in kimchi.
In their experiment, this bacteria stuck to the plastic in the gut.
After that, the plastic left the body more easily.
However, they tested mice, not people.
The news sounded exciting, and many websites shared it quickly.
But experts say we should be careful.
One study on mice is only a small first step.
Kimchi alone cannot solve the plastic problem.
The world still needs to make and throw away much less plastic.

B1.text:
Can Kimchi Save Us From Microplastics.
Kimchi, the fermented vegetable dish at the heart of Korean cooking, has long been praised for its health benefits.
It is rich in probiotics — the helpful bacteria that support digestion.
Recently, however, it has been connected to a much more modern problem: microplastics.
Microplastics are tiny fragments of plastic, often smaller than a grain of rice,
that form when larger plastic waste breaks down.
They have now been detected almost everywhere, including in drinking water, seafood, and even human blood.
Scientists are increasingly concerned about what they might do to our health over many years.
A study from the World Institute of Kimchi attracted a lot of attention.
Researchers isolated a single bacterium from kimchi and found that it could bind to plastic particles in the intestine.
In experiments with mice,
the animals that received this bacterium passed roughly twice as much plastic out of their bodies as those that did not.
The headlines were enthusiastic, suggesting that a popular side dish might quietly protect us.
But many experts urge caution.
The research was carried out on mice, used only one type of plastic,
and is still far from proven in humans.
More importantly, no diet can fix a problem this large.
The real solution is to produce far less plastic in the first place.

C1.text:
Why Kimchi Won't Save Us From Microplastics.
Kimchi occupies a near-mythical place in Korean food culture, celebrated not only for its sharp,
fermented flavour but also for a long list of supposed health benefits.
So when researchers suggested that a microbe found in kimchi might help rid the body of microplastics,
the story spread quickly — and, predictably, the coverage was glowing.
The science behind the buzz is genuinely intriguing.
Investigators at the World Institute of Kimchi isolated a lactic acid bacterium and demonstrated that,
under laboratory conditions designed to mimic the human gut, it clung to nanoplastic particles rather than releasing them.
In trials with mice, animals given the bacterium excreted roughly twice as much plastic as those that were not.
The implication was tantalising: that a familiar fermented food might double as a quiet detoxifier.
Yet enthusiasm should be tempered by what the study actually showed.
The work involved mice rather than people, tested a single type of plastic,
and took place in simulated rather than real digestive conditions.
Translating such findings into a meaningful human benefit is a long and uncertain road,
and many promising laboratory results never survive the journey.
There is also a deeper problem with the framing.
Microplastics are not a personal hygiene issue that individuals can simply eat their way out of;
they are a systemic consequence of how much plastic the world produces and discards.
Pinning our hopes on a side dish risks shifting responsibility away from the manufacturers and policies that drive plastic pollution.
Kimchi may be delicious and even modestly helpful,
but treating it as a cure lets the real culprits off the hook.
The only genuine remedy is to make, use, and waste far less plastic.

C2.text:
Kimchi Can't Save Us From Microplastics.
Few foods carry as much cultural weight as kimchi.
In Korea it is less a side dish than an institution,
and abroad it has been steadily rebranded as a fashionable "superfood," credited with everything from sharper immunity to a calmer gut.
So it was almost inevitable that, when scientists hinted kimchi might help flush microplastics from the body,
the claim would travel faster than the caveats attached to it.
The underlying research is far from frivolous.
A team at the World Institute of Kimchi isolated a strain of lactic acid bacterium and showed that,
in conditions engineered to approximate the intestine, it bound tenaciously to nanoplastic particles where rival microbes let go.
Mice given the strain excreted markedly more plastic — roughly double — than those left untreated.
As a piece of basic science, it is a perfectly respectable contribution to a young and urgent field.
The trouble lies not in the laboratory but in the leap from petri dish to dinner plate.
The experiments relied on mice, a single polymer, and a simulated gut; the messy reality of human digestion —
with its mixed meals, bile, enzymes, and resident microbial chaos — is another matter entirely.
Preliminary findings of this kind mark the beginning of a question, not the end of one,
and the graveyard of nutrition science is littered with compounds that dazzled in mice and disappointed in people.
More fundamentally, the story flatters a comforting but misleading idea:
that a problem manufactured at industrial scale can be undone by individual consumption.
Microplastics are not a personal failing to be corrected with the right breakfast;
they are the diffuse residue of a global economy built on disposable plastic.
Casting a fermented vegetable as the remedy quietly relocates responsibility from the corporations and regulators who shape plastic production onto the shoulders of ordinary eaters —
a sleight of hand that suits polluters rather well.
None of this means kimchi is worthless; it remains nourishing, probiotic-rich and, by most accounts, delicious.
But there is a meaningful difference between a food that is good for you and a cure for a planetary contamination crisis.
We cannot eat our way out of microplastics.
The only credible answer is to produce far less plastic and to dispose of what we do make with far greater care —
an unglamorous conclusion that no superfood headline will ever match.
